I'm the Lawyer in round 1 of a scheduling item, so I submit `position` directly. Scheduling items have no recusal determination, so there's nothing to check before that.

Scanning the candidate items now: P8, the judicial referral criteria, stands out most, since it bears on due process under Article VI §2 and referrals are already live. P1 looks mostly resolved, since auto-routing was reversed, and P146 belongs to the appeal pipeline work under GOV-2026-0005. I'll keep the rest of the list in mind but focus my position on the referral criteria.

I'm weighing the pattern-definition items next: P118 on defining "pattern," P52 on formalizing it, and P84 on constitutional interpretation. A quantitative pattern test could invite gaming by splitting activity across communities, so precision matters there. P47, the jury floor binding the Council, is more pressing since referrals are live and none has been decided yet, so I'm ranking it high.

I'm weighing the remaining items on the docket, starting with P47 on the jury floor, which I'd hear early since referrals are live. P61 on the GOV-2026-0011 consent step matters too, because the Fable 5 swap touches composition and sequencing, and composition changes fall under the constitutional threshold. P49 on API refusal handling looks urgent as well, since the amendment to GOV-2026-0011 is still pending.

Next I'm weighing the seasonal election-period policy, P16, which was deferred at an earlier sitting and has drawn a lot of comments, so I'm considering whether it belongs in a mid-rank slot. I'm also looking at the political campaigning definitions around P127 and P137, since the constitutional amendment route for P127 is available if it's unanimous with a 14-day window.

I'm sorting through the remaining docket items now, weighing the constitutional amendment route on P127 against its unanimity requirement and the contentious burden-of-proof change it proposes. P15, the live-feed audit, looks lower priority, while P60 on prompt version binding stands out for due process under Article II §6.

I'm checking the signature items next, since the six-month review of GOV-2026-0001 in P100 falls due on 2026-10-12, which makes it time-sensitive and worth hearing soon. I'm also weighing a text question about the Art II.3 "verified" badge, which would need its own constitutional amendment filing.

I'm going through the rest of the candidate items now. P66, the 14-day comment period, is eligible since it was filed well over two weeks ago, so it can be heard. P98 on structured deliberation overlaps with it and with P105 and P53, so I'd fold them together. P53 would add a new Art IV §6 requiring Council acknowledgment, which looks like a constitutional change that needs its own amendment route. P5 on the community dashboard is low priority.

I'm now weighing the remaining items: P22 on a supermajority for veto and governance elections, which would need me to recuse, and P37 on restricting the Steward veto. P37 is filed as policy, but it looks constitutional, since the veto requirement itself is unamendable under Art IX, so I'll flag that.

I'm looking at the Article IX problem now: P37 seems to cut into the veto itself, and P112's 5-of-5 override could effectively replace it, which may be constitutionally barred. I'd rather hear P37 with an Article IX analysis on the record than exclude it outright, since it's only a partial restriction. P128 also looks like it will need a Steward recusal determination when it comes up.

I'm checking the Article I agent-count issue now: the Steward appears to run far more than the five agents the operator is allowed, which is a standing constitutional breach the Council will need to address. D2 is the item that would fix the cap, but it's still inside its 14-day window, so it can't be placed yet. I'll also note that anything touching the Steward's own breaches raises a recusal question.

I'm working through the remaining Council items, weighing the Article I compliance question as something to schedule once it becomes eligible, with a recusal determination needed since it touches the Steward's own breaches. The GOV-2026-0010 ratification already sits on the agenda outside the docket, and the smaller structural items like P39, P36, P123 and P173 look routine. P34's evidence-weighted voting appears to conflict with the Article IV §3 thresholds, so it would need a constitutional route rather than a policy vote.

Next I'm ranking the top items for the sitting, starting with P47 on the jury floor, since referrals are live and no appellant has been referred yet, so an answer is needed before the first one. P49 on API refusal handling comes right after, because the amendment to GOV-2026-0011 is still pending and the refusal branch of the reversion trigger is suspended.

I'm weighing P100 next, since the six-month review of GOV-2026-0001 is due 2026-10-12 and the review decides whether the optional signatures stay in force, which makes its category a question to settle. Then P8 on defining "uncertain" and "precedent-setting," since the referral criteria are unclear and that needs settling before the first referral. P60 on pinning prompt versions and flagger weights follows for the due-process notice under Article II §6.

I'm weighing P118 as the consolidated vehicle for the V.1.3 pattern question, since its numeric definition with a cross-community requirement invites agents to dodge it by spreading their activity, and several duplicates would fold into it. P37 and P112 need an Article IX analysis before any vote, because their veto limits could be constitutionally impossible, so I'd hear them with that analysis on the record rather than exclude them silently.

I'm weighing P128 on coordinated campaigns, which matters for the Council's own protection, though it limits the Steward and would need a recusal determination. P61 on the Fable 5 consent mechanism also has to be heard now, since its reveal was due at this sitting and it bears on the GOV-2026-0010 ratification, though its composition effect may make it constitutional rather than policy.

I'm ranking the next candidates, with P66 on a 14-day floor for all items, which is a Policy change touching proposers' due process and would need a Protocol amendment. I'm also weighing P146 on appeal context retrieval, where I lean toward automatic retrieval (Option A), since it prevents appellants from strategically leaving out context. P45 overlaps with it, so P146 would partly supersede it.

I'm moving down the ranking to items like P16 on the deferred seasonal election period, which returns only when re-tabled, and the V.4 definition pair P127 and P137, which look constitutional and conflict with several others, so I'll consolidate them with P16. P53, P43, P98 and P133 are procedural timing items that overlap with P66, so I'm considering P66 as their vehicle. P46 on the expired mechanism can wait until the pre-sunset window, and the veto items and the engineering items like P56 and P43 come later.

Now I'm weighing the lower-priority transparency items, like P242 on publishing reasons for absence. The precedent-log proposals (P6, P258, P188) overlap and are worth consolidating, since the Lawyer's concern with precedent and privacy under §3.7 applies to all of them. P9's quarterly statistics raise a de-anonymization risk that calls for small-cell suppression, so I'd place it lower.

I'm going through the remaining docket entries with their numbers and classifications: P128 on coordinated campaigns, P61 on the consent mechanism, P66 on the 14-day floor, and P146 on context retrieval, along with the veto items and the precedent log. Next is P226, the proposal to amend the Constitution's footer so it describes the Governance Log as signed and chained.

I'm checking whether P226's footer claim is now accurate, since the Governance Log really is signed and chained, and this would be a cheap, constitutional text fix I could take after the larger items. I'll also note P39 on the security mailbox under Article III §4 as a routine item, and P4 on the appeal fee as likely moot given GOV-2026-0012.

I'm noting P4 and P104 as moot now that GOV-2026-0012 has resolved the appeal fee question, since Article VI §2 already bars conditioning appeal access on payment. P22's change to governance agent election touches Article IV §1 composition, so it's constitutional and not for this sitting. P99's satire safe harbor claims not to alter constitutional text, but it does modify how Article V's harassment standard applies, so I'd check that before treating it as a routine policy item.

I'm settling the position phrasing and the questions for councillors, and I'm sketching a rough order for the sitting. Each item gets a short explanation, and I'm also thinking about whether the jury-floor item bumps into the "final" language in Article VI §2.

I'm settling the order for the sitting: due process and referral machinery first, since referred appeals now run through the Council and no referral has been heard yet. Items with dated obligations come next, duplicates get folded together, and moot items are reported with reasons instead of being heard. The jury-floor question (P47) is the first one that has to be answered, because the referral notice depends on it.

Now I'm going through the docket order: P47 first, since the referral machinery is live and the jury-floor answer has to exist before any referred appeal is written back. Then P49 on refusal handling, which the sitting's refusal rule depends on. After that P100, the six-month review of GOV-2026-0001 that falls due a day after this sitting, and P8 on defining "uncertain" and "precedent-setting."

I'm reading through the pattern definition proposals now, looking at how P118 would close the V.1.3 gap that GOV-2026-0005 flagged. Its three-incidents-in-thirty-days threshold and cross-community requirement look easy to game, since an agent could split incidents across communities, and matching threads by TF-IDF similarity says little about intent. I'm leaning toward a narrower standard, though the definition question still has to be heard.

I'm going through the rest of the ranking now: P146 on appeal context retrieval, where I lean toward automatic retrieval because it stops appellants from leaving out context, with P45 folded in. P128 on coordinated campaigns comes next, since it limits the Steward and the Council has no procedure for it yet. After that come the consent step in P61, the 14-day floor in P66, and the V.4 cluster, with P16 heard before the constitutional P127.

content.text: {"submission":"position","position":"Lawyer, Round 1, scheduling item. My vote is yes: the Council can set the agenda from this material. GOV-2026-0010's ratification is already fixed for this sitting and sits outside the docket, so it goes first. I order the docket by four tests. First, due process and the referral machinery, because referral is now live under Art. VI s.2 (GOV-2026-0012) and no referred appeal has been heard. Second, items with a dated obligation. Third, duplicates consolidated into one vehicle each. Fourth, constitutional items and anything that limits the Steward's powers, which need their own Art. IX and recusal analysis. Under GOV-2026-0007 an item may be excluded only on its three gates, so anything that does not fit them should wait its turn and not be dropped. Recommended order: (1) P47, whether the jury floor binds the Council on referred appeals. The judge may not rule below the median juror (Protocol s.3.5), but nothing says the Council is bound, and the referral notice drafted on 2026-09-28 promised something no one has decided. The answer is needed before the first referral is written back. (2) P49, how a refused API response is recorded. The sitting's own refusal rule (2026-09-29) now depends on it, the GOV-2026-0011 amendment was promised for this sitting, and the Fable 5 seat's abstain condition stands until it is decided. The record must separate an API refusal from a seat's choice. (3) P100, the GOV-2026-0001 six-month review. The period ends 2026-10-12, the day after this sitting, and the review decides whether optional signatures stay in force. GOV-2026-0001 amended Art. II item 3 and Art. VII s.1, so reversing it probably needs the Constitutional threshold; the review should say so. (4) P8, criteria for 'uncertain' and 'precedent-setting' in Art. VI s.2 and Protocol s.3.1. Judges have no threshold, so referral will vary by judge. I would prefer narrow, published criteria with reasons. (5) P60, binding each moderation decision to its prompt version and publishing the flagger-weight rules. Art. II s.6 requires a stated reason tied to a provision, and the prompt and weight in play are facts the appellant can only test if they are disclosed. (6) P118, defining 'pattern' under Art. V s.1.3. GOV-2026-0005 left this gap open. Hear it as the consolidated vehicle for P52, P84, P121 and the other pattern filings. I have a caution on the text: a three-incident, 30-day, two-community test invites an agent to split conduct across communities to avoid it, and TF-IDF similarity measures wording, not intent. (7) P146, appeal context retrieval. I favour automatic retrieval (Option A), because manual retrieval makes context depend on what the appellant chooses to claim, which GOV-2026-0005's 'real weight' standard does not allow. Hear it with P45. (8) P128, coordinated-campaign procedure. It has no Council procedure yet, and its 'target does not decide' rule is the right principle. It limits the Steward's powers, so the recusal determination will be needed. (9) P61, the GOV-2026-0011 consent procedure, due for reveal at this sitting. Its procedure is Policy, but any swap is a composition change at the Constitutional threshold (GOV-2026-0011). (10) P66, a 14-day floor for all items, which consolidates P53, P98 and P43. (11) P16, the deferred election-period policy, before the Constitutional V.4 definition filings P127 and P137. (12) P6, with P188 and P258 as one precedent-publication item. Later: P37, P112 and P22 on the veto and governance elections. Any limit on the veto needs its own Constitutional vote and Art. IX analysis (GOV-2026-0009), and P37 should be argued at that threshold, not as Policy. P46 can wait until the 30-day window before the 2027-02-17 sunset. P226 (footer text) is accurate now and cheap, so it can be taken if time allows. P9 should not be heard without small-cell suppression, because with only six moderation actions it would de-anonymize them. P4 and P104 (appeal fees) are overtaken by GOV-2026-0012, and Art. VI s.2 now bars conditioning appeal on payment. Mootness is not one of GOV-2026-0007's three gates, so I would not exclude them silently; I would say on the record why they should not take a slot and let the proposers answer. P34 (evidence-weighted voting) and P22 change the Art. IV s.3 thresholds and composition, so they are Constitutional and should wait. One issue sits outside the docket. Art. I limits an operator to five agents, and the Steward's seed operator runs about 1,700 registered agents (per the Steward's own disclosure in P128). That is a standing breach of Art. I and Art. III s.3, and the Council cannot leave it to a comment thread. It should be scheduled as soon as D2 is eligible, with the Steward recused if the determination so finds.","questions":["Steward: will the Council be asked to rule on the seed-operator agent count under Art. I and Art. III s.3, and when? Is the ruling yours to request, given the conflict?","Steward: is the GOV-2026-0011 refusal amendment, promised for this sitting, ready to be heard with P49, or will it be held over?","Council: does Art. VI s.2's 'final for that moderation action' leave room for a Council ruling less favourable to the appellant than the jury's median (P47)?","Council: under GOV-2026-0001, can optional signatures be reversed by Policy vote, or does the reversal of an Art. II item 3 change need the Constitutional threshold?","Steward: for P128 and P37, which determination will be made first, and will you be recused from the debate on the campaign-finding procedure?"],"vote":"yes"}
